tldr: The authors propose "SG-CPG," an adaptive control framework that keeps quadruped locomotion stable under continuous actuator degradation. By keeping the healthy CPG policy frozen while applying severity-dependent stride shortening and whole-body re-coordination, the robot maintains its gait even under up to a 95% loss of torque.
hero_caption: Overall control architecture of SG-CPG. Combined with a frozen healthy CPG policy, a "residual gate" driven by degradation severity and an "amplitude gate" that shortens the weakened leg's stride work together to achieve both whole-body coordination compensation and joint load reduction.
overview:
When an animal hurts its leg, it does not simply give up walking. Instead, it unloads the injured limb and re-coordinates the remaining healthy legs to keep moving skillfully. Crucially, this adjustment happens smoothly according to the severity of the injury.

In contrast, most existing robotic fault-tolerance studies assume discrete "all-or-nothing" failures, such as a joint being completely locked or totally dead. However, continuous performance degradation—where torque limits gradually drop due to motor overheating, wear, or aging—has not been sufficiently addressed. In particular, for torque ceiling degradation (ceiling), an actuator behaves identically to a healthy one as long as commanded torque stays below the ceiling, creating an observational "deadband" that makes detection tricky.

To address this, the authors propose "SG-CPG." It keeps the healthy CPG (central pattern generator) policy frozen and introduces two severity-driven gates: an "amplitude gate" that physically shortens the weakened leg's stride to reduce demanded torque, and a single "residual gate" that rebalances the entire body across all legs, including the healthy ones.

Evaluated in simulation (Unitree Go2) and on a physical robot, SG-CPG achieved a 100% survival rate without falling across an omnidirectional command schedule even under a 95% torque ceiling loss in simulation. On the physical robot, it survived 28 out of 29 trials under up to a 93% torque reduction, demonstrating extremely robust adaptive performance.
contributions: Proposed "SG-CPG," a framework for continuous actuator degradation that preserves a frozen healthy CPG policy while combining severity-dependent stride shortening and whole-body re-coordination.

Formulated two distinct actuator degradation models—torque ceiling reduction (ceiling) and gain scaling (gain)—which possess different physical and observational properties, and developed adaptive policies for each.

Characterized the observational deadband associated with torque ceiling reduction, systematically comparing the accuracy and effectiveness of analytical methods versus learned models for severity estimation.
Demonstrated high sim-to-real transferability on a physical Unitree Go2, completing forward and turning motions almost perfectly even with up to 93% emulated torque degradation.

sections.heading: How do we handle actuators that "gradually weaken" rather than completely fail?
sections.summary: When vertebrates injure a limb, they reduce its load and re-coordinate their whole body based on injury severity. Because robots also suffer continuous torque loss from heating and wear, they need a CPG control system that adapts smoothly in proportion to severity rather than switching between discrete failure states.
sections.details:
Animal locomotion is supported not merely by top-down commands from the brain, but by rhythmic motions generated by neural circuits in the spinal cord called Central Pattern Generators (CPGs). When observing a cat with an injured paw or a limping dog, we see that they do not stop walking entirely. Instead, they reduce the load on the injured limb and rely on the remaining sound limbs to keep moving. In short, living organisms do not treat injury as a binary choice between healthy and failed; they perform graded adaptation scaled to the severity of the injury.

The same applies when robots operate outdoors for extended periods. Motor overheating and gearbox wear cause the maximum achievable torque to drop gradually. However, most prior fault-tolerant locomotion research has focused on extreme, discrete failures, such as a frozen joint or a completely severed limb.

A key challenge here lies in how degradation manifests physically. The authors focus on two mechanisms:

- Torque ceiling reduction (ceiling): Only the motor's maximum torque limit drops. As long as the demanded torque stays below this ceiling, the actuator behaves identically to a healthy one. This creates a "deadband" where the degradation cannot be observed from external behavior or sensors until heavy load causes torque clipping.
- Gain scaling (gain): The output torque of the controller is scaled down across the board. Because torque is attenuated at every single step, there is no deadband.

Especially under the former condition with an observational deadband, figuring out how to relieve the weakened leg while re-balancing the whole body across the other three legs becomes a critical problem. To solve this, the study proposes "SG-CPG," which leaves the healthy CPG policy completely intact and intervenes smoothly based on severity information.

sections.heading: What was missing at the intersection of CPGs, fault-tolerant locomotion, and residual learning?
sections.summary: Existing CPG learning and fault-tolerant control methods have largely focused on discrete leg failures or training separate policies for each specific leg. SG-CPG stands out by freezing the healthy locomotion policy and enabling severity-driven whole-body re-coordination through a single residual policy and an amplitude gate.
sections.details:
Examining related work helps clarify where this study fits in the broader landscape.

### II-A CPG-Based Locomotion Control
CPGs possess limit cycles (stable periodic orbits), allowing locomotion to be steered through intuitive parameters like phase, amplitude, and frequency. Recent works combine CPGs with deep reinforcement learning, such as CPG-RL, or explore inter-leg coupling, such as AllGaits. However, neither considers actuator performance degradation.

### II-B Fault-Tolerant Locomotion Control
Many fault-tolerant techniques have been proposed using self-modeling, behavior selection, and reinforcement learning, but most assume complete failures like locked joints. For instance, FT-CPG trains a dedicated residual policy for each individual failed leg. On the other hand, studies addressing continuous degradation, like FT-Net or ADAPT, only treat gain reduction and do not take the approach of intuitively attenuating gait through CPG amplitude control. Rather than dividing policies by leg, SG-CPG shares a single residual policy across all legs to achieve whole-body coordination.

### II-C Implicit Adaptation and Residual Policies
Methods like RMA (Rapid Motor Adaptation) estimate environmental and robot changes from proprioceptive history. However, the motor strength variations they assume during training are small (around 10%), and they do not directly account for the deadband caused by torque ceiling drops. Furthermore, conventional residual policy methods risk corrupting the healthy policy's behavior during training. In SG-CPG, when severity is zero, both the residual and amplitude gates close completely, structurally guaranteeing mathematically identical behavior to the healthy policy (structural preservation).

captions.F2: The overall SG-CPG pipeline. To modify the output of the frozen healthy CPG policy $\pi^h$, a single residual policy $\pi^d$ adjusts whole-body CPG parameters, foot trajectories, and joint position targets through a gate $g_d$ derived from severity $\alpha$. Simultaneously, the amplitude gate directly scales down the degraded leg's amplitude $\mu_i$.

sections.heading: A two-stage gating architecture: shorten the weakened stride and support with the rest
sections.summary: SG-CPG consists of a frozen healthy CPG, a single residual policy that corrects the whole body, and an amplitude gate that directly shortens the stride of the weakened leg. It defines torque ceiling and gain drops as degradation mechanisms, and validates online severity estimators.
sections.details:
The design for keeping a degraded robot walking smoothly is clear and rational.

### III-A CPG Formulation
Each leg $i$ is assigned an amplitude-controlled phase oscillator. The policy outputs a per-leg amplitude target $\mu_i$, frequency $\omega_i$, secondary phase rate $\psi_i$, phase offset $\phi^{\mathrm{off}}_i$, and inter-leg coupling weights $w$. Because the fore-aft foot swing amplitude is determined by the product of step length and oscillator amplitude $(r_i - 1)$, lowering $\mu_i$ directly shrinks the leg's physical reach.

### III-B Two Actuator Degradation Mechanisms
The severity of joint $j$ is denoted as $\alpha_{ij} \in [0, 1)$, where 0 is healthy and 0.99 is near-total loss.

- Torque ceiling reduction (ceiling): The joint's PD gains are preserved, but the maximum torque limit $L_j$ is lowered to $(1 - \alpha_{ij}) L_j$. While demanded torque remains below this limit, motion is identical to healthy behavior, creating a deadband where sensors cannot detect the fault.
- Gain scaling (gain): The overall output torque of the PD controller is multiplied by $(1 - \alpha_{ij})$. Torque is attenuated at every time step, so no deadband exists.

### III-C Gated Residual Composition
Once trained, the healthy policy $\pi^h$ has its parameters completely frozen. When a degradation occurs, a single residual policy $\pi^d$ engages. The residual gate $g_d$ acts globally across all legs because when one leg weakens, the other three healthy legs must step up to support the body. The residual offsets are added at three points: CPG parameters, foot trajectory shapes (clearance and swing phase ratio), and post-IK joint position targets.

### III-D Severity-Amplitude Gate (Amplitude Gate)
This is a key innovation of the method. The degraded leg's amplitude target $\tilde{\mu}_i$ is directly scaled by $(1 - \bar{\alpha}_i)$. In other words, as severity increases, that leg's stride automatically shortens. A smaller stride lowers the demanded torque-angle product, drastically cutting the frequency of hitting the lowered torque ceiling.

### III-E Severity Estimation
During training, the true severity (oracle) is provided. For real-world deployment, the authors evaluate both an analytical estimator that calculates severity from past peak torques and learned estimators using CNNs, Transformers, and MLPs.

sections.heading: Demanding omnidirectional command schedules and realistic simulation design
sections.summary: Simulations were conducted on a Unitree Go2 in Isaac Lab with 100 Hz control and 1 kHz physics. Survival rates and velocity tracking errors were rigorously evaluated not just on straight paths, but through tough omnidirectional schedules combining lateral, backward, and turning motions, along with perturbation tests.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation and Training Environment
The Isaac Lab physics simulator was used to train the Unitree Go2 quadruped on flat ground. The control loop runs at 100 Hz, and physics simulation runs at 1 kHz. Motor nominal torque limits are 23.70 Nm for hip swing and thigh, and 45.43 Nm for the knee (calf).

Policies were trained with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). The healthy policy $\pi^h$ was rewarded for velocity tracking and base stability. The residual policy $\pi^d$ was trained by slightly relaxing posture penalties while granting a stride amplitude bonus. As a baseline, a configuration zeroing direct base linear velocity observations (ZBLV: a perturbation-robust model) was also prepared.

During training episodes, a single random joint's severity was reduced to a fixed value during the first 3 seconds. The severity was uniformly sampled between the onset of clipping and 0.99.

### IV-B Evaluation Protocol
Because merely standing still to endure a fault does not count as true walking, this study evaluates both "survival rate (not falling)" and "velocity tracking error" together.

- Forward sweep: 20-second runs across 13 severity levels $\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, \ldots, 0.95, 0.97, 0.99\}$ for each of the 12 joints individually.
- Omnidirectional sweep: Extending the FT-CPG protocol, this challenging 25-second episode rapidly switches commands among forward (0.5 m/s), lateral (0.4 m/s), in-place turning (0.6 rad/s), and diagonal walking.
- Robustness tests: With a degraded knee joint, the policy was evaluated under friction variations, added payloads, PD gain variations, joint velocity noise, and lateral push perturbations.

sections.heading: Maintaining a trot even after losing 95% torque! What ablations reveal about each gate
sections.summary: In simulation, SG-CPG maintained a 100% survival rate during omnidirectional walking even under a 95% torque ceiling drop, keeping tracking error around 8%. Ablation analysis clearly showed that the amplitude gate drastically cuts torque saturation while severity observation guarantees survival.
sections.details:
### V-A Simulation Results: Gait Preservation and Tracking Performance
In the forward sweep, all four policies maintained a trot gait even at $\alpha=0.99$ (a state with almost zero torque capacity). In the omnidirectional sweep, even under the severe condition of $\alpha=0.95$, SG-CPG achieved a 100% survival rate and kept command tracking error around 8% (and within 16.0% across all commands). Omnidirectional walking proved far more challenging than straight-line tests, bringing true fault tolerance to light.

### V-B Physical Differences Between Degradation Mechanisms
Under torque ceiling reduction (ceiling), demanded torque stayed within limits up to $\alpha=0.5$, resulting in a 0% median clipping rate. At $\alpha=0.9$, however, torque saturated (clipped) during 35.1% of steps. Under gain scaling (gain), the entire torque was constantly attenuated, resulting in a consistent 0% clipping rate. This confirms the presence of the "deadband" in ceiling faults.

### V-C Robustness to Perturbations
The robot survived all 40 out of 40 trials under low friction and joint velocity noise. However, when an added payload (+5 kg) coincided with softened gains, falls occurred on certain legs, exposing the limits under extreme loading conditions.

### V-D Can Severity Be Estimated?
Interestingly, under torque ceiling reduction (ceiling), a simple analytical estimator based on past peak torques achieved an MAE (0.007) more than four times lower than learned models like CNNs or Transformers. The peak torque observed the moment the ceiling is hit provides the most direct and accurate reflection of the degradation level.

### V-E Ablation Study (Comparing A1 and A2)
To examine the role of each design component, two ablations were tested:

- A1 (Severity-Blind Residual): The severity input $\alpha$ to the residual policy was removed.
- A2 (No Amplitude Gate): The severity input was kept, but the stride $\mu_i$ was not scaled down.

Under the ceiling condition at $\alpha=0.8$, the fraction of steps where the weakened joint hit its torque ceiling (clipping rate) surged from 4.4% in SG-CPG to 13.6% in A1 and 26.3% in A2. This demonstrates that without the amplitude gate (A2), excessive torque demands on the joint cannot be prevented, and without severity information (A1), survival rates drop.

sections.heading: Validation on a real Unitree Go2: surviving 28 of 29 trials with 93% torque loss
sections.summary: SG-CPG was tested on a physical Go2 by clamping position error on the front-right knee to emulate a torque limit. It survived 28 of 29 trials under up to 93% torque degradation, and the amplitude gate drastically reduced base tilt from 7.0 degrees down to 2.8 degrees.
sections.details:
The findings from simulation were deployed onto a real Unitree Go2 robot. Because the motor API lacks a direct torque limit setting, a torque ceiling reduction (ceiling) was emulated by clamping the position error.

- Healthy transfer: In the absence of faults, SG-CPG matched the healthy policy $\pi^h$ perfectly, achieving 87% to 100% of commanded velocities measured via ground tape.
- Survival envelope at 93% degradation: Under extreme conditions with 85% to 93% torque loss on the front-right knee (calf), the robot recorded an impressive survival rate of 19 out of 20 trials in forward walking (up to 1.0 m/s) and 9 out of 9 trials in turning (up to 1.0 rad/s), totaling 28 out of 29 survived trials.
- Importance of the residual during thigh degradation: When the thigh joint was degraded to $\alpha=0.80$, turning off the residual gate caused the robot to fall within 4 seconds, exceeding the 34.4-degree tilt limit. When the residual was enabled, the robot walked stably across all 4 trials while maintaining an average tilt of 2.6 to 3.2 degrees.
- Dramatic effect of the amplitude gate: At $\alpha=0.85$, the amplitude gate alone halved the average base tilt from about 7.0 degrees to 3.6–3.9 degrees and reduced the fraction of time spent in torque saturation from 77% to around 39%. Combining this with the residual policy's corrections allowed the robot to recover speed while keeping tilt at 2.4 to 3.1 degrees.
- Actuator system identification: To bridge the sim-to-real gap, motor friction and stiffness were identified from physical actuator responses and incorporated into retraining. This eliminated high-frequency command chattering (power spectral density above 8 Hz dropped from 0.61 to 0.05), resulting in smooth walking.

sections.heading: Summary: moving beyond discrete failure switching toward continuous robot adaptation
sections.summary: SG-CPG establishes a framework that smoothly adapts to continuous actuator degradation without compromising the healthy locomotion policy. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of severity-driven stride shortening and whole-body re-coordination.
sections.details:
This paper introduced "SG-CPG," an adaptive control framework that maintains quadruped locomotion under the challenging scenario of continuous actuator degradation in a single joint.

By freezing the healthy CPG policy and combining a severity-driven residual gate with an amplitude gate that directly relieves the weakened limb's workload, the design achieves smooth adaptation in a single unified architecture without needing separate policies for different severities or legs.

Even when facing severe torque drops of 95% in simulation and 93% on a real Go2, the robot completed omnidirectional trajectories while maintaining a trot gait. For robots operating in real-world environments over long periods, performance degradation due to component wear or motor overheating is inevitable. Moving past conventional approaches that simply halt or trigger special fallback modes upon failure, SG-CPG paves a practical, elegant path for robots to embrace their own physical wear and carry on with their missions.

takeaways: Adding residual corrections via a "severity gate" while keeping the healthy policy frozen provides fault tolerance without sacrificing any healthy walking performance.
Because torque ceiling reduction (ceiling) exhibits a deadband, an analytical method based on maximum torque in an observation window estimates severity more accurately than learned models.

Simply shortening the stride of the degraded leg (amplitude gate) halves both joint torque saturation and body tilt, showing that intuitive CPG parameter control is an excellent fit for fault tolerance.
Straight-line walking tests in simulation tend to overestimate fault-tolerant capabilities, making evaluation on demanding omnidirectional and turning schedules essential.
limitations: Evaluations in this study are limited to flat ground; adapting to torque degradation on rough terrain or stairs remains future work.
The method was evaluated on single-joint degradation, and behavior under compound failures—such as multiple degraded legs or multiple weakened joints on the same leg—has not been tested.

In closed-loop online estimation on the physical robot, the estimator tended to underestimate severity (predicting around 0.37 against a true value of 0.85), indicating that a sim-to-real gap in real-world severity estimation still remains.
